questions.prompt: During his earthly ministry, how many men did Jesus choose to be his closest followers, the Apostles?
choices: Twelve
Seven
Ten
Seventy
questions.explanation: Jesus chose twelve, deliberately echoing the twelve tribes of Israel -- a sign that he was gathering and renewing God's people, not starting something with no connection to what came before.
questions.hint: The number deliberately echoes the twelve tribes of Israel.

citations.quote: he called his disciples to himself, and from them he chose Twelve, whom he also named apostles

questions.prompt: True or False: At the Last Supper, Jesus instituted the Eucharist, commanding the apostles to do this in memory of him.
questions.explanation: True. Jesus took bread and wine, identified them as his body and blood, and commanded his apostles to repeat the action -- the origin of the Mass, celebrated by the Church ever since.
questions.hint: This is the same meal the Church still re-enacts at every Mass.

citations.quote: Then he took the bread, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which will be given for you; do this in memory of me.'

questions.prompt: Before ascending into heaven, Jesus commanded the apostles: 'Go, therefore, and make disciples of all ____, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy Spirit.'
questions.explanation: This command, known as the Great Commission, is why the Church's mission was never meant to stay confined to one people or one land -- it points outward, to the whole world, from the very start.
questions.hint: The command is not to one people but to every one of them.

citations.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: What happened forty days after Jesus' Resurrection, according to the Gospels and Acts?
choices: He ascended into heaven before his apostles' eyes
He was crucified a second time
He returned permanently to ordinary life on earth
He appeared only to strangers who did not know him
questions.correctAnswer: He ascended into heaven before his apostles' eyes
questions.explanation: The Ascension closes Jesus' visible earthly presence and opens the waiting period the apostles spend together in Jerusalem before Pentecost -- the very next event in the Church's story.
questions.hint: This is Jesus' final visible departure, watched by the apostles themselves.

citations.quote: When he had said this, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him from their sight.

questions.prompt: True or False: Before ascending, Jesus told his apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the coming of the Holy Spirit.
questions.explanation: True. Jesus told the apostles not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for 'the promise of the Father' -- a waiting period that ends at Pentecost, the Church's next major event.
questions.hint: He tells them to wait for something still to come, in the very city they are already in.

citations.quote: he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for 'the promise of the Father about which you have heard me speak'

questions.prompt: Match each moment in Jesus' ministry to what it established for the Church that would follow.

pairs.right: A structured leadership echoing the twelve tribes of Israel
The Eucharist, repeated at every Mass since
A mission sent to every nation, not one people alone
Jesus' visible presence ends; the wait for the Spirit begins

questions.explanation: Before the Church takes any action of its own, Jesus himself lays every piece of its foundation -- leaders, sacrament, mission, and the promise of the Spirit still to come.
questions.hint: Each item on the left is something Jesus does; match it to what it sets up for later.

citations.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: What does the Catechism say stands at the center of what the apostles, and the Church after them, are sent to proclaim?
choices: The Paschal mystery of Christ's cross and Resurrection
A set of purely ethical teachings with no reference to Christ
The political restoration of Israel as a nation
A private philosophy meant only for a small elite
questions.correctAnswer: The Paschal mystery of Christ's cross and Resurrection
questions.explanation: Everything the apostles will go on to preach, and everything this whole topic will trace across the centuries, radiates outward from this one center: Christ's death and Resurrection.
questions.hint: It is the same event the Church still calls the heart of the Gospel.

citations.quote: The Paschal mystery of Christ's cross and Resurrection stands at the center of the Good News that the apostles, and the Church following them, are to proclaim to the world.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Gospels describe the apostles as confident and unshaken throughout Jesus' arrest and crucifixion.
questions.explanation: False. The Gospels are strikingly honest about the apostles' failure -- they scattered, and Peter denied even knowing Jesus three times. That failure makes what happens to them at Pentecost, in the next level, all the more remarkable.
questions.hint: Consider what the Gospels themselves say happened at Gethsemane and during Peter's questioning in the courtyard.

citations.quote: And they all left him and fled

questions.prompt: Jesus' descent into hell and Resurrection reveal, as the Catechism puts it, that it was precisely out of the depths of ____ that he made life spring forth.
questions.explanation: This is the event the whole apostolic mission flows from -- life breaking open from within death itself, which is exactly what the apostles will spend the rest of their lives proclaiming.
questions.hint: The place Christ's Resurrection breaks life out of.

citations.quote: The Apostles' Creed confesses in the same article Christ's descent into hell and his Resurrection from the dead on the third day, because in his Passover it was precisely out of the depths of death that he made life spring forth

questions.prompt: Taken together, what do the Twelve, the Eucharist, the Great Commission, and the Ascension have in common?
choices: All were established by Jesus himself, before the Church took a single action of its own
All were decisions made later by the apostles without Jesus' involvement
All happened only after several centuries of Church development
None of them appear anywhere in the New Testament
questions.correctAnswer: All were established by Jesus himself, before the Church took a single action of its own
questions.explanation: This level's whole point is that the Church does not invent its own foundation -- leadership, sacrament, mission, and the promise of the Spirit are all set in place by Christ himself, before Pentecost, before a single apostle acts on his own initiative.
questions.hint: Who is the one common actor behind everything covered in this level?

citations.quote: The Paschal mystery of Christ's cross and Resurrection stands at the center of the Good News that the apostles, and the Church following them, are to proclaim to the world.

questions.prompt: According to strong and ancient tradition, which apostle carried the Gospel as far as India?
choices: Thomas
James the Less
Bartholomew
Philip
questions.explanation: Tradition holds that Thomas -- remembered for doubting the Resurrection until he touched Christ's wounds -- carried the Gospel to India, where communities tracing their origin to him, the Saint Thomas Christians, exist to this day.
questions.hint: This is the same apostle remembered for doubting the Resurrection until he touched Christ's wounds.

citations.quote: Thomas answered and said to him, 'My Lord and my God!'

questions.prompt: True or False: The Apostle Paul undertook multiple missionary journeys across the eastern Mediterranean, founding churches in cities like Corinth, Philippi, and Ephesus.
questions.explanation: True. Paul's journeys, recorded in Acts and reflected in his own letters, planted churches across Asia Minor and Greece -- several of which he later wrote back to, correcting and encouraging communities he had personally founded.
questions.hint: These are the same cities whose churches later received his letters.

citations.quote: he left Athens and went to Corinth

questions.prompt: Tradition holds that the Apostle Mark founded the Church in which major city, becoming its first bishop?
choices: Alexandria
Athens
Carthage
Damascus
questions.explanation: Mark, whose Gospel drew on Peter's own preaching, is traditionally remembered as the founder of the Church in Alexandria, Egypt -- a see that becomes one of the ancient world's most important centers of Christian learning.
questions.hint: This city in Egypt becomes one of the ancient world's great centers of Christian learning.

citations.quote: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greeting, as does Mark, my son.

questions.prompt: The city of ____, in modern-day Syria, is where the disciples of Jesus were first called 'Christians,' according to the Acts of the Apostles.
questions.explanation: Antioch becomes one of the earliest and most important centers of the apostolic Church -- Peter himself is remembered as its first bishop before later tradition sends him to Rome.
questions.hint: This same city later becomes one of the great ancient patriarchal sees.

citations.quote: it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians

questions.prompt: Match each apostle to the region tradition most strongly associates him with.

pairs.right: India
Alexandria, Egypt
Antioch, then Rome
Ephesus, then Patmos

questions.explanation: Within a single generation, apostolic preaching reaches from Rome in the west to India in the east -- the mission Christ gave at the Ascension already in visible motion.
questions.hint: One apostle's exile produces the Church's last biblical book, written on an island.

citations.quote: I found myself on the island called Patmos because I proclaimed God's word and gave testimony to Jesus.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to Church tradition, John is the only one of the Twelve Apostles believed to have died of natural causes rather than martyrdom.
questions.explanation: True. Tradition holds John, exiled to Patmos but not killed there, lived to old age in Ephesus -- the sole exception among the Twelve to a pattern of violent death that this whole topic will keep returning to.
questions.hint: Every other apostle's traditional death is violent; this one's is not.

citations.quote: I found myself on the island called Patmos because I proclaimed God's word and gave testimony to Jesus.

questions.prompt: What does the rapid spread of apostolic preaching, from Rome to India within a single generation, suggest about the early Church's own self-understanding?
choices: It understood itself as sent to the whole world, not confined to one people or land
It understood itself as a purely local movement meant to stay in Jerusalem
It actively avoided contact with any culture outside Judea
It had no coordinated sense of mission at all
questions.correctAnswer: It understood itself as sent to the whole world, not confined to one people or land
questions.explanation: This is the Great Commission from level 1, already visibly in motion -- apostles individually carrying the Gospel to Rome, Egypt, Asia Minor, and India, each independently acting on the same universal mandate.
questions.hint: Recall the command Jesus gave in level 1's Great Commission.

citations.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: True or False: Paul described himself as having been called to be an apostle even though he was not one of the original Twelve.
questions.explanation: True. Paul, converted after persecuting the Church, describes himself as an apostle 'set apart for the gospel of God' -- proof that the apostolic mission was never limited only to the original Twelve.
questions.hint: He describes his own calling in the opening lines of several of his letters.

citations.quote: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God

questions.prompt: According to Church tradition, the Apostle James the Greater traveled and preached as far as ____, in the western reaches of the Roman world.
questions.explanation: Whether or not every detail of the tradition is historically verifiable, it reflects the same pattern this level keeps tracing -- apostolic mission reaching to the furthest edges of the known world within a single lifetime.
questions.hint: This western European country's patron saint tradition traces back to this apostle.

citations.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain

questions.prompt: Why does this level matter for understanding what comes next in the Church's story?
choices: Because the sees the apostles planted become the centers the rest of this topic keeps returning to
Because none of these missionary journeys had any lasting institutional effect on the wider Church at all
Because the apostles' travels were completely unrelated to where later bishops and councils would ever be based
Because the early Church actively discouraged any lasting contact between these distant regions
questions.correctAnswer: Because the sees the apostles planted become the centers the rest of this topic keeps returning to
questions.explanation: The next level asks how the faith these apostles planted gets handed on after they die -- and the answer runs directly through the sees this level has just mapped: Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, and the rest.
questions.hint: Think ahead to what has to happen once these apostles themselves eventually die.

citations.quote: it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians

questions.prompt: What does the Church call the process by which the apostles' own authority was handed down to the bishops who came after them?
choices: Apostolic succession
Papal infallibility
Sacred Tradition alone, with no office involved
Ecumenical council
questions.explanation: Apostolic succession is precisely the mechanism this level traces: bishops, ordained in unbroken lines going back to the apostles themselves, so that apostolic teaching authority does not die out with the apostles' own deaths.
questions.hint: The name of this doctrine describes bishops literally succeeding the apostles.

citations.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Irenaeus of Lyons could list, by name, the successive bishops of Rome going back to the apostles who founded that church.
questions.explanation: True. Writing in the second century, Irenaeus lists the bishops of Rome one by one from the apostles down to his own day -- direct, named evidence that apostolic succession was a real, traceable chain, not a later legend.
questions.hint: This second-century writer treats the succession as a real, named, traceable list.

citations.reference: St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies
citations.quote: The blessed apostles, then, having founded and built up the Church, committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate... In this order, and by this succession, the ecclesiastical tradition from the apostles... have come down to us.
In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: According to St. Irenaeus, the apostles who founded the Church in Rome committed the office of the episcopate into the hands of ____, its first successor as bishop.
questions.explanation: Linus is the first named link in an unbroken chain Irenaeus can trace all the way to his own day -- exactly the kind of concrete, named evidence that makes apostolic succession something historians can actually examine, not just a claim taken on faith alone.
questions.hint: The first name in Irenaeus's own list of Roman bishops after the apostles.

citations.reference: St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies
citations.quote: The blessed apostles, then, having founded and built up the Church, committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate... In this order, and by this succession, the ecclesiastical tradition from the apostles... have come down to us.

questions.prompt: St. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 107 AD on his way to martyrdom, taught that the Church gathers around what central figure in each local community?
choices: The bishop
The oldest living member
A rotating council with no fixed head
Whichever wealthy patron funds the community
questions.explanation: Ignatius, a bishop himself and a direct link to the apostolic generation, insists the bishop is where Christ's own Church becomes visible in each place -- one of the earliest clear statements of the structure apostolic succession was building.
questions.hint: This second-century bishop ties the Church's very presence to one particular office.

citations.reference: St. Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans
citations.quote: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or term to what it contributes to understanding apostolic succession.

pairs.right: Insists the bishop is where the Church is visibly present
Names the actual chain of bishops back to the apostles
The first successor to the apostles as bishop of Rome
States the Church's own doctrine of why bishops succeed the apostles

questions.explanation: Together these four pieces make apostolic succession something more than an abstract claim -- a named chain of real men, defended by writers who were themselves close to the apostolic generation, and taught as doctrine by the Church today.
questions.hint: Two are individual writers, one is a name in a list, one is the Church's own current teaching.

citations.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Second Vatican Council taught that the college of bishops has authority only when understood together with the successor of Peter as its head.
questions.explanation: True. Even twenty centuries later, the Council restates the same shape this level has been tracing from the beginning -- bishops acting as a body, but always in communion with Peter's successor, never independently of him.
questions.hint: The Council ties the bishops' authority together with one particular office, the same one from level 1.

citations.quote: the college or body of bishops has no authority unless it is understood together with the Roman Pontiff, the successor of Peter as its head.

questions.prompt: According to Lumen Gentium 8, the Church that Christ established, and that the apostles handed on, subsists concretely in what?
choices: The Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him
No visible institution at all, only an invisible spiritual reality
A purely local congregation with no wider connection
Whichever community happens to hold the largest membership at a given time
questions.correctAnswer: The Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him
questions.explanation: This is the twentieth-century Council restating, in its own words, the exact claim apostolic succession makes: the Church Christ founded remains identifiable, governed today by the same structure -- Peter's successor and the bishops -- that this level has traced back to Linus and the apostles themselves.
questions.hint: The Council names a specific, still-existing structure of governance.

citations.quote: This Church constituted and organized in the world as a society, subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him

questions.prompt: St. Ignatius of Antioch wrote that wherever the ____ appears, there the multitude of the people should be also, just as wherever Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
questions.explanation: For Ignatius, unity with the bishop is not administrative convenience -- it is how the Church's own unity with Christ becomes visible in a given place, a principle apostolic succession exists to protect.
questions.hint: The office this level has centered on from Linus to Ignatius to Lumen Gentium.

citations.reference: St. Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans
citations.quote: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
the college or body of bishops has no authority unless it is understood together with the Roman Pontiff, the successor of Peter as its head.

questions.prompt: Why does this level matter for what comes next: the Church's story returning, in the next level, to Peter, Pentecost, and the very first Christian community?
choices: Because that structure is what preserved the Pentecost-era Church's teaching long enough for us to study it now
Because apostolic succession has no real connection whatsoever to Pentecost or the first community
Because the very next level abandons everything about structure that was just covered here
Because bishops as an office only appear in Church history many centuries after Pentecost itself

What this level has just shown is why that early community's faith did not simply vanish with the apostles' deaths: bishops like Linus were already carrying it forward even as it happened.
questions.hint: Consider what makes it possible to know anything reliable about the Pentecost-era Church at all, this many centuries later.

citations.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: Match each level of this topic's opening arc to its central concern.

The apostles individually carry the Gospel across the known world
Bishops succeed the apostles so the faith survives their deaths
A closer look at Peter, Pentecost, and the earliest Christian community

questions.explanation: These four levels are one continuous argument: Christ founds it, the apostles spread it, the bishops preserve it, and only then does the topic slow down to examine the earliest community in detail -- because by level 4, a learner already knows why that community's faith reached us at all.
questions.hint: The topic moves from foundation, to spread, to preservation, before it slows down to look closely at the beginning.

citations.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: According to the Gospel of Matthew, what name did Jesus give to Simon, declaring him the 'rock' on which he would build his Church?
choices: Peter
Andrew
James
Bartholomew
questions.explanation: Jesus renamed Simon 'Peter' (from the word for 'rock') and gave him the keys of the kingdom -- a foundational moment for the papacy that the Church continues to teach today.
questions.hint: Names in the Gospels carry meaning -- this one means 'rock' in Greek.

citations.quote: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of the netherworld shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys to the kingdom of heaven.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catholic Church teaches that when the original apostles died, their teaching authority died with them.
questions.explanation: The Church teaches the opposite: the apostles left bishops as their successors so that 'the full and living Gospel might always be preserved' -- a doctrine known as apostolic succession.
questions.hint: The apostles didn't leave the Church leaderless -- think about who they appointed to carry on their authority.

citations.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

questions.prompt: The Acts of the Apostles describes the very first Christian community in Jerusalem as devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, and the breaking of the bread, along with which fourth practice?
choices: The prayers
Fasting alone
Public debate
Almsgiving alone
questions.explanation: Acts 2:42 gives this fourfold pattern -- teaching, fellowship, the breaking of the bread, and prayer -- which the Catechism points to as a model of Christian communal life from the Church's earliest days.
questions.hint: It's the fourth item Acts 2:42 lists, right after 'the breaking of the bread.'

citations.quote: They devoted themselves to the teaching of the apostles and to the communal life, to the breaking of the bread and to the prayers.
The faith of the faithful is the faith of the Church, received from the apostles.

questions.prompt: Match each New Testament letter to the church its opening verses say it was written to.

pairs.right: The church in Rome
The church in Corinth
The church in Ephesus
The church in Philippi

questions.explanation: Paul's letters are addressed to real, named local churches he founded or hoped to visit -- the New Testament grew out of pastoral correspondence to specific communities, not abstract treatises.
questions.hint: Each letter's very first verse names the city it's addressed to.

questions.prompt: Jesus told Peter that whatever he bound or loosed on earth would be bound or loosed in ____.
questions.explanation: This promise of binding and loosing, given to Peter and later to the apostles as a group, is the scriptural root of the Church's teaching authority passed down through apostolic succession.
questions.hint: It completes the same phrase Jesus already used about binding and loosing.

citations.quote: I will give you the keys to the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Apostle Paul was one of Jesus' original Twelve Apostles, chosen during his earthly ministry.
questions.explanation: Paul was not one of the Twelve. He was a persecutor of the Church who was called by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, years after Jesus' ascension.
questions.hint: This apostle wasn't called until after the Ascension, on a road trip that went dramatically wrong.

questions.prompt: On the day of Pentecost, described in Acts 2, what happened to the apostles?
choices: They received the Holy Spirit and began preaching boldly in many languages
They fled the city of Jerusalem entirely, in fear of the authorities
They were promptly arrested and imprisoned by the Sanhedrin on the spot
They quietly returned home to their former fishing occupations
questions.correctAnswer: They received the Holy Spirit and began preaching boldly in many languages
questions.explanation: Pentecost is the Church's birthday: the same men who had scattered at Christ's arrest now preach publicly without fear, in languages understood by pilgrims from many nations. That reversal is itself part of the evidence something real had happened to them.
questions.hint: The same apostles who scattered in fear at Jesus' arrest suddenly speak boldly in front of crowds -- and pilgrims from many nations understand every word.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15, decided that Gentile converts did not need to be circumcised according to the Mosaic Law.
questions.explanation: True, and it is the first council in Christian history. The apostles gathered, deliberated, and issued a decision binding on the whole Church — a small-scale preview of every ecumenical council that followed.
questions.hint: Acts 15 settles a very practical question: does a Gentile convert need to become Jewish first?

questions.prompt: According to tradition, where were Peter and Paul both martyred?
choices: Rome
Jerusalem
Antioch
Corinth
questions.explanation: Both apostles died in Rome under Nero, which is part of why the Roman church has always held a place of particular honor — she is the church where two of the greatest apostles gave their lives.
questions.hint: Both apostles died under the same Roman emperor, Nero, in the empire's capital.

pairs.right: A lasting mark of honor on the Roman church
The Church's first martyr

questions.hint: One is about power given, one about a boundary removed, one about a place honored, one about a first death.

questions.prompt: Before Christians had dedicated church buildings, where did the earliest communities most commonly gather to worship?
choices: In ordinary homes, called house churches
In former pagan temples, immediately repurposed
In large public stadiums rented for the occasion
Exclusively in the Jerusalem Temple
questions.correctAnswer: In ordinary homes, called house churches

questions.hint: Paul's own letters greet the church meeting inside a particular person's household.

questions.prompt: True or False: Early Christian communities were made up mostly of the wealthy and powerful, with little presence among the poor or enslaved.
questions.explanation: False. Paul himself reminds the Corinthians that not many of them were wise, powerful, or of noble birth by the world's standards -- the early Church drew heavily from the poor, the enslaved, and the socially marginal alongside a smaller number of the wealthy.
questions.hint: Paul reminds one community directly about their own social standing before their calling.

citations.quote: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. Rather, God chose the foolish of the world to shame the wise

questions.prompt: Writing around 155 AD, St. Justin Martyr's First Apology describes the Christian Sunday assembly as including which elements?
choices: Readings from the 'memoirs of the apostles,' a common prayer, and the president giving thanks over bread and wine
A strictly private household ritual conducted with no readings, prayers, or shared meal at all
A public liturgy held only once each year, on a fixed pagan civic holiday
A loosely organized gathering with no single set leader presiding over any part of it
questions.correctAnswer: Readings from the 'memoirs of the apostles,' a common prayer, and the president giving thanks over bread and wine
questions.explanation: Justin's account -- one of the earliest outside descriptions of a Christian Sunday liturgy -- already shows readings, a homily, common prayers, and thanksgiving over the gifts: recognizably the same shape the Mass still holds today.

questions.prompt: True or False: Under Roman law before Constantine, being identified as a Christian could be treated as a capital offense, even without any other crime alleged.

questions.prompt: What did new converts typically undergo before being admitted to baptism in the pre-Constantinian Church?

Immediate baptism with no prior instruction of any kind
A mandatory donation of all personal property

questions.prompt: Why were Christians in the Roman Empire frequently accused of atheism?
choices: They refused to worship the emperor or the traditional Roman gods, which pagans understood as a rejection of the gods entirely
They openly and repeatedly denied the existence of any god or divine power whatsoever, in every public setting
They refused, as a firm and unbending matter of religious principle, to ever build temples of any kind
They rejected outright, in all of their public teaching and private practice, the very concept of any afterlife
questions.correctAnswer: They refused to worship the emperor or the traditional Roman gods, which pagans understood as a rejection of the gods entirely
questions.explanation: From the Roman side, refusing to honor the recognized gods looked exactly like atheism — worshipping an invisible God nobody else recognized did not register as worship at all to outside eyes. The charge reveals as much about Roman categories as about Christian belief.
questions.hint: Ask what 'atheism' meant to a Roman, not what it means today.

questions.prompt: True or False: Roman persecution of Christians was a single continuous policy enforced uniformly across the whole empire for three centuries.
questions.explanation: False. Persecution was sporadic and regional for most of this period — intense under some emperors, absent under others, often driven by local officials or mob pressure rather than a standing imperial policy. The empire-wide persecutions under Decius and Diocletian were the exception, not the norm.
questions.hint: Ask whether every emperor in this period actively persecuted Christians.

questions.prompt: The Roman catacombs served primarily as underground ____ for Christians, not as hiding places from persecution as popular legend often claims.
questions.explanation: Roman law actually protected burial places, including Christian ones, even during persecution — the catacombs were legally recognized cemeteries. The romantic image of Christians hiding for Mass in the catacombs during raids is largely a later invention.
questions.hint: Ask what Roman law actually protected, regardless of a group's religion.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the age of the martyrs to its meaning.

Christians who denied the faith under persecution to save their lives

questions.explanation: The last term matters because it created a real pastoral crisis: what should happen to a lapsed Christian who later wanted to return? That question shaped the early Church's whole theology of penance and reconciliation.
questions.hint: Three of these describe faithful responses to persecution; one describes a failure of nerve under it.

questions.prompt: What is the modern name historians give to Emperor Diocletian's empire-wide persecution of Christians, begun in 303 AD?
choices: The Great Persecution
The Edict of Toleration
The Diocletian Reforms
The Nicene Crisis
questions.explanation: Diocletian's campaign was the most systematic and severe persecution in the Church's first three centuries -- churches destroyed, Scriptures confiscated and burned, clergy imprisoned. It is also, strikingly, the last major persecution before everything changes.
questions.hint: This is remembered as the most severe and systematic of all the Roman persecutions.

citations.quote: Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to tradition, Constantine saw a vision before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 that led him to fight under a Christian symbol.
questions.explanation: True. Tradition holds Constantine saw a sign in the sky -- a cross or the Chi-Rho -- along with words often rendered 'in this sign, conquer,' and had his soldiers mark their shields accordingly before defeating his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge.
questions.hint: This vision comes before a decisive battle for control of Rome itself.

questions.prompt: Is the claim that 'Constantine invented the divinity of Christ' historically accurate?
choices: False -- Christ's divinity is attested throughout the New Testament, centuries before Constantine was born
True -- there is no evidence Christians believed Christ was divine before the 4th century
True, but only among a small minority of Christians before Nicaea
False, but only because Constantine himself denied ever making the claim
questions.correctAnswer: False -- Christ's divinity is attested throughout the New Testament, centuries before Constantine was born
questions.explanation: This is one of the most persistent popular myths about this period. John's Gospel, written some two and a half centuries before Nicaea, already opens by calling the Word God -- belief in Christ's divinity long predates any Roman emperor's involvement in Church affairs.
questions.hint: Consider how early the New Testament itself already speaks of Christ.

citations.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

questions.prompt: Emperor Constantine ____ the Council of Nicaea in 325, but it was the assembled bishops who actually defined what the Church believed there.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters: an emperor could call bishops together and pay for their travel, but he could not settle a question of doctrine himself. Confusing the two is exactly what produces the popular myth this level has already addressed.
questions.hint: What an emperor can do -- call a meeting -- is different from what only bishops can do there.

questions.prompt: True or False: Constantine was baptized immediately after his conversion in 312, decades before his death.
questions.explanation: False. Constantine, following a common practice of the era, deferred his baptism until he was near death in 337 -- a reminder that his own relationship to the faith was gradual and, by later standards, unusual, even as his political decisions transformed the Church's situation.
questions.hint: Consider how long Constantine actually waited between his vision in 312 and his death.

questions.prompt: According to tradition, what did Constantine's mother, St. Helena, discover on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem?
choices: Relics of the True Cross
The original manuscripts of the four Gospels
The tomb of the Apostle Peter
The Ark of the Covenant
questions.explanation: Helena's pilgrimage, and the churches she helped build in the Holy Land, are part of the same transformed situation this level traces -- pilgrimage and public veneration of holy sites were simply impossible under active persecution.
questions.hint: Her discovery is tied to the very instrument of Christ's death.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or event from this level to what it represents in the shift from persecution to legality.

pairs.right: The empire's harshest persecution, immediately before everything changes

pairs.left: Constantine's vision at the Milvian Bridge
pairs.right: The moment tradition credits with turning an emperor toward Christianity
Imperial support for a council, not imperial authorship of doctrine
Public Christian veneration newly possible under a changed political climate

questions.explanation: None of these four things could have happened as recently as Diocletian's own reign -- the whole level traces how quickly, and how incompletely, the Church's situation actually changed within a single generation.
questions.hint: Order them by how quickly the political situation shifts across this level.

questions.prompt: True or False: Constantine's shift toward Christianity made the empire's religious situation immediately and fully settled, with no further controversy to come.
questions.explanation: False. Legality did not mean unity -- the very next level covers the Council of Nicaea, called precisely because a serious internal dispute, Arianism, needed to be settled once Christians were finally free to gather openly and debate it.
questions.hint: Consider what the very next level in this topic is actually about.

questions.prompt: Given everything this level covers, what is the most accurate way to describe the political shift Constantine brought about?
choices: A shift from active persecution to legal toleration and imperial favor -- not an instant, complete transformation of doctrine or unity
A shift in which Constantine personally authored and permanently settled every point of Christian doctrine himself
A shift that brought no real practical consequences of any kind at all for ordinary Christians
A shift that immediately and permanently ended all theological disagreement of any kind within the whole Church
questions.correctAnswer: A shift from active persecution to legal toleration and imperial favor -- not an instant, complete transformation of doctrine or unity
questions.explanation: This is the level's central corrective: Constantine changed the Church's legal and political situation dramatically, but he neither invented Christian belief nor settled Christian doctrine -- both errors this level has already directly addressed.
questions.hint: Weigh what changed (legal status) against what did not (who defines doctrine).

questions.prompt: Now able to gather openly for the first time in the Church's history, bishops soon convened at ____ in 325 to settle a serious dispute over the nature of Christ.
questions.explanation: This is exactly the handoff this level sets up: legal freedom to assemble is what makes an ecumenical council -- bishops from across the empire gathering in one place -- possible for the very first time.
questions.hint: The city that gives the next level, and its famous creed, their name.

questions.prompt: The First Council of Nicaea, held in 325 AD, was convened primarily to address which controversy?
choices: The Arian heresy, which denied the full divinity of Christ
The date on which Easter should be celebrated each year
The final canon of the Old Testament's books
The specific civil authority of the Bishop of Rome
questions.correctAnswer: The Arian heresy, which denied the full divinity of Christ
questions.explanation: Arius taught that the Son was a created being, not truly God. Nicaea gathered bishops from across the Church to condemn this teaching and affirm Christ's full divinity.
questions.hint: This heresy denied Christ was fully God -- answering it was Nicaea's whole purpose.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: The Nicene Creed professes that the Son is '____ with the Father,' affirming that he is fully and truly God.
questions.explanation: 'Consubstantial' translates the Greek 'homoousios' -- of the same substance -- the precise word Nicaea chose to rule out any reading of Christ as a lesser, created being.
questions.hint: This word is the English translation of the Greek 'homoousios.'

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Council of Nicaea in 325 AD produced the complete Nicene Creed exactly as it is prayed at Mass today, including its section on the Holy Spirit.
questions.explanation: Nicaea produced an earlier, shorter creed focused on the Son's divinity. The fuller text prayed today, including the extended article on the Holy Spirit, was completed at the First Council of Constantinople in 381.
questions.hint: A later council, decades after Nicaea, finished the Creed's article on the Holy Spirit.

citations.quote: And in the Spirit, the holy, the lordly and life-giving one, proceeding forth from the Father, co-worshipped and co-glorified with Father and Son, the one who spoke through the prophets.

questions.prompt: The Council of Chalcedon in 451 AD defined that Christ has two natures, fully divine and fully human, united in one ____.
questions.explanation: This is the hypostatic union: one divine Person, Jesus Christ, possessing two complete natures without confusion or division.

questions.prompt: What changed for the Church in 313 AD with the Edict of Milan?
choices: Christianity was granted legal toleration throughout the Roman Empire, ending centuries of periodic persecution

The Bishop of Rome was newly granted direct civil authority over the whole of Italy
questions.correctAnswer: Christianity was granted legal toleration throughout the Roman Empire, ending centuries of periodic persecution
questions.explanation: Milan granted toleration, not establishment — Christianity became one legal religion among others, not yet the empire's exclusive faith. That distinction is easy to blur, and getting it right avoids overstating how quickly the political situation actually changed.
questions.hint: Toleration and establishment are two different things — which one happened in 313?

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Monica prayed for her son Augustine's conversion for many years before it finally happened.
questions.explanation: True. Augustine describes his mother's decades of prayer and tears in the Confessions, and her perseverance became a model held up for anyone praying for a wayward loved one across a very long time.

questions.prompt: St. Benedict of Nursia founded the monastery of Monte ____ around 529 AD, and his Rule became the foundation of Western monasticism.

questions.prompt: St. Anthony of Egypt, often called the father of Christian monasticism, is traditionally said to have withdrawn into the desert after hearing which Gospel passage read at Mass?

"Love your enemies and pray sincerely and constantly for those who persecute you"

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Jerome translated the Old Testament portion of the Vulgate directly from the Hebrew, against significant opposition, including from St. Augustine.
questions.explanation: True. Augustine worried that departing from the familiar Greek Septuagint would unsettle congregations; Jerome went to the Hebrew text anyway. Even two of the era's greatest minds could disagree openly and at length -- the Fathers were not a uniform bloc.

questions.prompt: St. Ambrose of Milan baptized the future Doctor of the Church St. ____ of Hippo in 387 AD, after years of preaching that helped bring about his conversion.
questions.explanation: Ambrose's preaching in Milan was instrumental in winning over the restless heart Augustine himself describes in his Confessions -- one bishop's influence reshaping the whole future of Western theology.
questions.hint: Ambrose's preaching wins over the author of the Confessions.

questions.prompt: Dei Verbum 25 quotes St. Jerome's maxim, in Latin 'Ignoratio Scripturarum ignoratio Christi est.' What does this claim?

Knowledge of Scripture replaces the need to know Christ personally
The Scriptures are too difficult for ordinary believers to read
Christ can only be known apart from the Scriptures
questions.correctAnswer: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ
questions.explanation: This fourth-century maxim mattered enough to the Second Vatican Council that it quotes Jerome directly, urging frequent reading of Scripture -- a patristic voice given fresh authority some fifteen centuries later.
questions.hint: The same word appears twice in the Latin, once about Scripture and once about Christ.

questions.prompt: True or False: Pope St. Gregory the Great signed his letters 'Servant of the servants of God,' a title still used by popes today.
questions.explanation: True. 'Servus servorum Dei' expressed Gregory's conviction that the papacy itself is an office of humble service -- a vision that centuries later shapes how the Second Vatican Council speaks of every ordained minister, not only the pope.
questions.hint: This title deliberately puts service, not power, at the center of the office.

questions.prompt: In 1964, Pope Paul VI gave St. Benedict of Nursia what title, honoring his role in shaping Western monastic and cultural life?
choices: Patron of Europe
Doctor of the Church
Universal Patron of Workers
Patron of the Missions
questions.explanation: Benedict's Rule -- balancing prayer and manual labor -- shaped monastic life so deeply across the continent that Paul VI named him Patron of Europe centuries after his death, a mark of how far this movement's influence eventually reached.
questions.hint: Benedict's influence stretched across an entire continent, not just Italy.

questions.prompt: Beyond copying Scripture, monasteries in the early medieval West also preserved and copied the surviving works of pagan ____ and Roman literature, keeping much of ancient learning from being lost entirely.
questions.explanation: Monastic scriptoria became, almost as a side effect of copying Scripture and the liturgy, one of the main reasons any classical literature survives to be read today at all -- a debt the medieval universities of a later level will build directly on.
questions.hint: Monks preserved more than just Christian texts in their scriptoria.

questions.prompt: Match each figure of this level to what he contributed to the Christian West.

questions.prompt: True or False: Christian mission during this period was limited entirely to the territory of the former Roman Empire, with no expansion beyond its old borders.
questions.explanation: False. Missionaries such as St. Patrick carried the Gospel to Ireland, well beyond the empire's old frontier, planting a monastic Christian culture that would itself later send missionaries back into a Europe unsettled by Rome's collapse.

citations.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Taken together, what does this level's picture of monks, translators, preachers, and missionaries suggest about the Church in the centuries after Constantine?
choices: Legal freedom let the Church build durable institutions -- monasteries, translated Scripture, mission -- that would outlast the Roman Empire itself
The Church became entirely and permanently dependent on the Roman imperial state for its own basic survival
Monastic life had no lasting cultural or intellectual influence on the West beyond private, individual prayer
Missionary activity stopped almost completely across the whole Church once active persecution had formally and finally ended
questions.correctAnswer: Legal freedom let the Church build durable institutions -- monasteries, translated Scripture, mission -- that would outlast the Roman Empire itself
questions.explanation: This is the level's real payoff: the freedom won in level 7 was not just freedom from persecution, but freedom to build -- and what got built here (monasteries, the Vulgate, a reformed vision of the papacy, missions beyond Rome's own borders) proved durable enough to carry the faith through Rome's coming collapse, which the next level turns to directly.
questions.hint: Consider what these institutions were still doing long after the Roman Empire itself was gone.

questions.prompt: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne with what title?
choices: Emperor of the Romans
King of the Franks alone, with no imperial title
Patriarch of the West
Duke of Aachen

questions.prompt: True or False: Charlemagne's coronation by the Pope created a partnership between crown and Church, not a simple subordination of one to the other.
questions.explanation: True, and the tension in that partnership -- who ultimately holds authority when crown and papacy disagree -- becomes a recurring theme across the medieval centuries this level opens, not something settled once and for all at Charlemagne's coronation.

citations.quote: Then repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God.

questions.prompt: Charlemagne sponsored a revival of learning, manuscript copying, and education across his empire, remembered by historians as the Carolingian ____.
questions.explanation: This deliberate revival built directly on the monastic scriptoria of level 9 -- Charlemagne's court actively recruited scholars and funded the copying of texts that had been quietly preserved through the centuries since Rome's fall.
questions.hint: The same word later used for the much larger cultural revival of the 15th century.

questions.prompt: Alcuin of York, a scholar invited to Charlemagne's court, is remembered chiefly for what contribution?
choices: Leading the revival of learning and education across Charlemagne's empire
Leading a military campaign against the Byzantine Empire
Translating the Bible into the Frankish vernacular for the first time
Founding the first medieval university at Paris
questions.correctAnswer: Leading the revival of learning and education across Charlemagne's empire
questions.explanation: Alcuin, an English monk and scholar, became the intellectual center of Charlemagne's court, organizing schools and standardizing texts -- the human engine behind the Carolingian Renaissance this level has just named.
questions.hint: He is the human engine behind the revival of learning just described in this level.

questions.prompt: Match each term or figure from Charlemagne's reign to what it involved.

pairs.right: Revived an imperial title in the West, tied to the papacy
