questions.explanation: All four pieces of this level point the same direction: a deliberate, court-sponsored effort to recover and spread learning that had survived only precariously in scattered monasteries since Rome's fall.
questions.hint: One is a coronation, one is a person, one is a handwriting style, one is the whole movement they add up to.

questions.prompt: True or False: Carolingian minuscule, developed during this period, made manuscripts significantly easier to read and copy accurately.
questions.explanation: True. This clearer, more standardized script -- distinguishing upper and lower case more consistently than earlier styles -- reduced copying errors and is part of why so many ancient texts survive today in legible form.
questions.hint: Think about what a clearer, more standardized handwriting style would do for a text passed hand to hand across many copyists.

questions.prompt: What happened to Charlemagne's empire after his death in 814?
choices: It fractured among his heirs, contributing to centuries of political fragmentation in Western Europe
It remained fully and firmly unified under a single heir for the next two full centuries
It was immediately and completely absorbed into the rival Byzantine Empire
It dissolved entirely and abruptly, leaving behind no successor states of any kind
questions.correctAnswer: It fractured among his heirs, contributing to centuries of political fragmentation in Western Europe
questions.explanation: The empire's division among Charlemagne's grandsons at the Treaty of Verdun (843) set the rough shape of what would later become France and Germany -- and left medieval Western Europe politically fragmented for centuries, a backdrop this topic's next several levels will keep returning to.
questions.hint: Consider what political shape Western Europe has for most of the rest of the medieval period this topic covers.

questions.prompt: When Jesus was asked about paying taxes to Caesar, he answered: repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to ____ what belongs to God.
questions.explanation: This principle -- a real distinction, and a real relationship, between civil authority and God's claim -- is exactly what Charlemagne's coronation puts into new practical tension: an emperor crowned by a pope, ruling a kingdom, under a King whose kingdom is not of this world.
questions.hint: The second half of Jesus' answer names the one whose claim is not Caesar's.

citations.quote: Then repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God.

questions.prompt: True or False: Charlemagne's imperial coronation permanently and cleanly settled every question about the relationship between royal and papal authority.
questions.explanation: False. Far from settling the question, it opened it -- disputes over the relative authority of pope and emperor would recur throughout the medieval period, including in the East-West tensions the next level turns to and the investiture conflicts of later centuries.
questions.hint: Consider whether this same tension keeps reappearing across the rest of this topic's medieval levels.

questions.prompt: While Charlemagne's coronation strengthened ties between Rome and the Frankish West, what was happening, over these same centuries, to Rome's relationship with the Christian East?
choices: It was gradually growing more distant, in language, custom, and authority, setting up the split the next level covers
It was growing rapidly closer and more fully unified with each passing decade of this period
It had already been fully and formally severed a full century earlier than this
The Christian East itself had already ceased to exist entirely by this period
questions.correctAnswer: It was gradually growing more distant, in language, custom, and authority, setting up the split the next level covers
questions.explanation: Charlemagne's coronation itself was part of what strained relations with Constantinople -- crowning a Western emperor implicitly rivaled the existing Roman emperor still ruling from the East. The next level picks up exactly this gradual drift, tracing it to its formal rupture in 1054.
questions.hint: Consider how crowning a new 'Roman' emperor in the West might look from Constantinople, where a Roman emperor already reigned.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Great Schism of 1054 was primarily caused by a single theological dispute settled in one dramatic confrontation, with no earlier history of tension.
questions.explanation: False. The mutual excommunications of 1054 were the culmination of centuries of gradually diverging practice, language, and authority between Rome and Constantinople -- the Filioque dispute was real, but it was not a sudden rupture out of nowhere. Reading it as one clean break misses the slow drift level 10 already began tracing.
questions.hint: Ask whether centuries of difference in language, custom, and authority preceded 1054, or appeared only that year.

questions.prompt: In 1054, what actually happened between Rome and Constantinople that is remembered as the Great Schism?
choices: Papal legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople exchanged mutual excommunications
The Pope formally and permanently dissolved the Church in the East
The Byzantine Emperor expelled every Christian from Constantinople
The two sides signed a permanent treaty of full reunion
questions.correctAnswer: Papal legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople exchanged mutual excommunications
questions.explanation: Papal legates placed a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the Patriarch responded in kind. Neither act by itself instantly created the full, lasting separation that followed -- but it formalized a rupture that centuries of gradual drift had already been building toward.
questions.hint: This is a formal, mutual act -- not a war, a treaty, or a unilateral expulsion.

questions.prompt: One real theological dispute behind the schism concerned the ____, a phrase added to the Latin Creed describing the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the Father and the Son.
questions.explanation: The Eastern Church objected both to the theological claim and to the West's unilateral addition of a word to a creed formulated by an ecumenical council -- a dispute this whole topic has already prepared a learner to recognize, since it goes back to the Nicene Creed covered in level 8.
questions.hint: Latin for 'and the Son' -- the phrase added describing the Spirit's procession.

questions.prompt: Match each event to its role in the long history of East-West relations.

pairs.right: Restored the veneration of icons in the East
The formal act remembered as the Great Schism
A brief, unsuccessful attempt to reunite East and West
Another short-lived reunion, later repudiated in the East

questions.explanation: Centuries of real, serious effort -- twice formalized in council -- still could not produce a lasting reunion between East and West, a sobering pattern this level asks a learner to actually sit with rather than skip past.
questions.hint: Two of these attempted reunion; one restored icons; one names the split itself.

citations.quote: the honour paid to an image traverses it, reaching the model, and he who venerates the image, venerates the person represented in that image.

questions.prompt: True or False: The mutual excommunications of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople were formally lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras.
questions.explanation: True. The mutual anathemas were consigned to oblivion in a joint declaration during the closing period of the Second Vatican Council. Lifting them did not restore full communion -- the underlying theological differences remained -- but it removed a formal obstacle that had stood for nine centuries.
questions.hint: This gesture came during the final year of a twentieth-century ecumenical council covered later in this topic.

questions.prompt: What is the state of communion between the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Churches today, despite genuine efforts toward reunion?
choices: Full, lasting communion has still not been restored, though relations have warmed considerably
Full communion was completely restored by the 1965 lifting of the mutual excommunications
The two communions have had no meaningful contact since 1054
The schism was fully healed at the Council of Florence in 1439
questions.correctAnswer: Full, lasting communion has still not been restored, though relations have warmed considerably
questions.explanation: The Second Vatican Council renewed the Catholic Church's own commitment to seeking unity with the East, but the schism first formalized in 1054 remains -- an honest, unresolved wound this level does not pretend has already been healed.
questions.hint: Distinguish 'warmer relations' from 'restored communion' -- they are not the same thing.

citations.quote: The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.

questions.prompt: The Council of Florence in 1439 produced a short-lived reunion between East and West that was later ____ in the East, showing how fragile these agreements proved.
questions.explanation: Political pressure -- Constantinople's leaders sought Western military help against the advancing Ottoman Turks -- helped produce the Florence agreement, but it never gained real acceptance among Eastern clergy and laity once that pressure eased.
questions.hint: What happens to an agreement once the people it was meant to bind refuse to accept it.

questions.prompt: True or False: Language and cultural differences between the Latin-speaking West and Greek-speaking East played no real role in the growing estrangement that led to 1054.
questions.explanation: False. By the eleventh century, most Western clergy could no longer read Greek and most Eastern clergy could no longer read Latin -- a practical barrier to genuine ongoing theological communication that compounded the real doctrinal disputes rather than standing apart from them.
questions.hint: Consider whether clergy on each side could still easily read the other side's own theological writing by this period.

questions.prompt: Given everything this level has shown -- centuries of drift, one formal rupture, two failed reunions, and a still-open wound today -- what is the most accurate summary of East-West relations across this whole history?
choices: A slow estrangement, formalized once, that repeated sincere efforts have not yet been able to fully heal
A sudden, single event in 1054 that both sides immediately and permanently accepted as final
A dispute that was fully and completely resolved by the Second Vatican Council
A conflict with no real theological substance behind it at all
questions.correctAnswer: A slow estrangement, formalized once, that repeated sincere efforts have not yet been able to fully heal
questions.explanation: This level's honesty matters: the Church does not pretend an unresolved wound is resolved. Holding that tension is itself part of what this topic is teaching -- not every chapter of Church history ends in tidy resolution.
questions.hint: Weigh 'gradual and still unresolved' against 'sudden and already settled.'

questions.prompt: Meanwhile, in the Latin West during these same centuries, what new kind of institution and new kind of religious movement were beginning to take shape?
choices: The medieval university and the mendicant, preaching religious orders
The first Christian monasteries of any kind, appearing for the very first time
A complete rejection of all formal education and learning
The permanent abolition of all religious orders founded earlier
questions.correctAnswer: The medieval university and the mendicant, preaching religious orders
questions.explanation: While East and West grew further apart, the Latin West was undergoing its own real transformation -- universities organizing higher learning and new orders like the Franciscans and Dominicans reshaping religious life, which the next level turns to directly.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: What documented context, beyond a simple claim of unprovoked aggression, preceded the First Crusade in 1095?
choices: Centuries of prior territorial conquest and a direct appeal from the Byzantine Emperor for military help against Turkish advances
No prior context of any kind at all -- the Crusades simply began with no history behind them whatsoever
A centuries-old, mutually cordial, formal military alliance between Rome and the Turkish Sultanate
A single unanimous request from every bishop in the Christian East for total, unrestrained war
questions.correctAnswer: Centuries of prior territorial conquest and a direct appeal from the Byzantine Emperor for military help against Turkish advances
questions.explanation: This real documented context does not by itself justify every action taken during the Crusades -- some of which, like the 1204 sack of Constantinople, the Church has itself acknowledged and apologized for -- but a flattened 'purely unprovoked' framing omits it entirely.
questions.hint: Consider who specifically asked for military help, and why.

citations.quote: Injustice, excessive economic or social inequalities, envy, distrust, and pride raging among men and nations constantly threaten peace and cause wars.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Church has never publicly acknowledged wrongdoing connected to events like the Crusades.
questions.explanation: False. Pope St. John Paul II publicly asked forgiveness for sins committed by members of the Church throughout history at a 'Day of Pardon' liturgy during the Jubilee Year 2000 -- a real, documented act of public repentance, not silence or denial.
questions.hint: Consider a specific public liturgy held during the Jubilee Year 2000.

citations.reference: Day of Pardon liturgy, Pope St. John Paul II (2000)

questions.prompt: What was the primary purpose of the medieval university, as institutions like Paris and Bologna developed during this same period?
choices: To organize the systematic study of theology, law, medicine, and the arts under a structured curriculum with degrees
To train soldiers specifically and exclusively for military service in the ongoing Crusades
To replace monastic life entirely across the whole of Western Europe
To serve exclusively the sons of the reigning nobility and no one else
questions.correctAnswer: To organize the systematic study of theology, law, medicine, and the arts under a structured curriculum with degrees
questions.explanation: The university is a medieval Christian invention, growing out of cathedral schools -- the degree structure, faculties, and much of the vocabulary of higher education today descend directly from this period.
questions.hint: Ask what institution still exists today, using much of the same vocabulary this period invented.

questions.prompt: St. Francis of Assisi founded a religious order built on radical poverty, later known as the Friars ____.
questions.explanation: Francis's charism was a literal, radical embrace of poverty as gospel witness -- give away what you have and follow Christ -- taken up by a movement that spread with striking speed across thirteenth-century Europe.
questions.hint: Latin for 'lesser' or 'little' brothers -- the order's own official name.

citations.quote: Jesus said to him, 'If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to [the] poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.'

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Dominic founded the Order of Preachers specifically to combat the Albigensian heresy through sound teaching and preaching.
questions.explanation: True. Where Francis's charism answers attachment to possessions, Dominic's answers doctrinal confusion directly -- his order is literally named for the activity, the Order of Preachers, still called Dominicans today.
questions.hint: This founder's whole order is literally named for the activity his charism is fitted to.

citations.quote: The personal charism of some witnesses to God's love for men has been handed on... so that their followers may have a share in this spirit... In their rich diversity they are refractions of the one pure light of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Match each 12th- and 13th-century development to what it involved.

pairs.right: Launched partly in response to Byzantine appeals and prior territorial loss
Organized theology, law, medicine, and the arts under a formal degree system
Founded the Friars Minor on radical poverty
Founded the Order of Preachers to answer doctrinal confusion

questions.explanation: This level holds two very different stories side by side on purpose -- real violence with real documented context on one hand, and a genuine flowering of learning and new religious life on the other. Both are honestly part of the same century.
questions.hint: Two of these are about the Crusades and universities; two are about new religious orders.

citations.quote: Injustice, excessive economic or social inequalities, envy, distrust, and pride raging among men and nations constantly threaten peace and cause wars.

questions.prompt: What term describes religious orders like the Franciscans and Dominicans, who -- unlike earlier monks bound to one monastery -- traveled and ministered among the wider population?
choices: Mendicant orders
Cloistered orders
Military orders
Contemplative-only orders
questions.explanation: 'Mendicant' comes from the Latin for 'begging' -- these friars owned little to nothing personally and depended on alms, freeing them to travel and preach in the growing medieval towns and the new universities alike, rather than remaining fixed in one monastery like earlier Benedictine monasticism.
questions.hint: The word comes from the Latin for 'begging.'

citations.quote: Jesus said to him, 'If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to [the] poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.'

questions.prompt: True or False: The rise of universities and mendicant orders in this period were entirely unrelated developments with no real connection to each other.
questions.explanation: False. Dominicans and Franciscans became deeply involved in the new universities themselves, teaching and studying there -- the two developments this level covers actually reinforced each other, not two unrelated stories placed side by side by coincidence.
questions.hint: Consider where friars like Dominicans actually went on to teach.

questions.prompt: The Church's own 2000 Jubilee Year 'Day of Pardon' liturgy shows that acknowledging real historical wrongs and genuinely teaching the ____ are not in tension with each other.
questions.explanation: Honest engagement with a complicated history -- neither an uncritical defense nor a flattened accusation -- is itself part of what this level, and this whole topic, is modeling for a learner.
questions.hint: The thing this whole app exists to teach, which honest history does not actually threaten.

citations.reference: Day of Pardon liturgy, Pope St. John Paul II (2000)

questions.prompt: Given the mendicant orders' deep involvement in the new universities this level has described, what kind of intellectual synthesis does the next level explore?
choices: Scholasticism -- the disciplined use of reason to explore and defend the faith, most famously in St. Thomas Aquinas
A total and complete rejection of reason itself in favor of pure, unreflective faith alone
A complete and deliberate break from every single prior Church Father's own teaching
A synthesis with no meaningful connection at all to the universities just described here
questions.correctAnswer: Scholasticism -- the disciplined use of reason to explore and defend the faith, most famously in St. Thomas Aquinas
questions.explanation: Aquinas himself was a Dominican, formed by exactly the combination this level has traced -- mendicant order and university -- and his work becomes the next level's whole subject.
questions.hint: Consider what order the next level's central theologian actually belonged to.

citations.quote: The personal charism of some witnesses to God's love for men has been handed on... so that their followers may have a share in this spirit... In their rich diversity they are refractions of the one pure light of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Which 13th-century theologian's philosophy was later commended by Pope Leo XIII as a model for Catholic teaching?
choices: St. Thomas Aquinas
St. Augustine of Hippo
St. Anselm of Canterbury
St. Bonaventure
questions.explanation: Leo XIII's 1879 encyclical Aeterni Patris held up Aquinas's synthesis of faith and reason -- worked out inside the new university system level 12 just described -- as a lasting model for Catholic philosophy and theology.
questions.hint: His massive theological synthesis is still studied in seminaries today.

citations.quote: restore the golden wisdom of St. Thomas, and to spread it far and wide for the defense and beauty of the Catholic faith

questions.prompt: St. Thomas Aquinas's major work synthesizing faith and reason is called the Summa ____.
questions.explanation: The Summa Theologiae remains one of the most influential works of Catholic theology, systematically working through the whole of Christian doctrine -- and it was written, taught, and debated inside the university system level 12 just introduced.
questions.hint: It's the same theologian named in the previous question's encyclical.

citations.quote: the Fathers of Trent made it part of the order of conclave to lay upon the altar, together with sacred Scripture and the decrees of the supreme Pontiffs, the Summa of Thomas Aquinas, whence to seek counsel, reason, and inspiration.

questions.prompt: St. Anselm of Canterbury, writing a century before Aquinas, summarized theology's basic task in a phrase often translated as what?
choices: Faith seeking understanding
Reason replacing faith entirely
Faith with no role for reason at all
Understanding that requires no faith whatsoever
questions.explanation: Anselm's phrase, 'fides quaerens intellectum,' captures the whole scholastic project this level covers: reason is not opposed to faith but works from within it, seeking to understand more deeply what is already believed.
questions.hint: Faith comes first in this phrase, and reason follows, working from inside it.

questions.prompt: True or False: Scholastic theologians like Aquinas structured their major works around a formal method of stating objections before answering them.
questions.explanation: True. The Summa Theologiae's own structure -- an article poses a question, lists objections, then answers each in turn -- is not incidental decoration; it is the scholastic method itself, disputatio, taking objections seriously rather than ignoring them.
questions.hint: Look at how the Summa Theologiae itself is actually laid out, article by article.

questions.prompt: The scholastic method of formally debating a theological question -- stating objections, then resolving them -- is known in Latin as the ____.
questions.explanation: This method grew directly out of the university classroom level 12 just introduced -- a real, structured practice of public academic debate, not simply a private way of writing.
questions.hint: The Latin word this method is named for, sharing a root with the English word 'dispute.'

questions.prompt: St. Bonaventure, a leading Franciscan theologian and near-contemporary of Aquinas, represents what alongside Aquinas's Dominican approach?
choices: A distinct Franciscan scholastic tradition, showing Scholasticism was never a single uniform school of thought
A complete and total rejection of Aquinas's entire method by the whole Franciscan order itself
An identical theology with no meaningful differences from Aquinas's own theology at all
A separate tradition existing entirely outside the university system this level has already described
questions.correctAnswer: A distinct Franciscan scholastic tradition, showing Scholasticism was never a single uniform school of thought
questions.explanation: Bonaventure, minister general of the Franciscans, developed real theological emphases of his own alongside Aquinas's Dominican synthesis -- a useful reminder that 'Scholasticism' names a shared method and setting, not one single, uncontested set of conclusions.
questions.hint: Consider which order this Franciscan theologian belonged to, alongside Dominican Aquinas.

citations.quote: The personal charism of some witnesses to God's love for men has been handed on... so that their followers may have a share in this spirit... In their rich diversity they are refractions of the one pure light of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or term of Scholasticism to what it represents.

pairs.right: 'Faith seeking understanding,' theology's basic scholastic task
The formal method of stating and resolving objections
The Dominican synthesis of faith and reason in the Summa
A distinct Franciscan scholastic tradition alongside Aquinas's

questions.explanation: Together these show Scholasticism as a real intellectual movement with real internal diversity -- a shared method and setting (the university, the disputatio) producing genuinely different theological schools, not one single voice.
questions.hint: Two of these are individual theologians from different orders; two are the shared method and its motto.

questions.prompt: True or False: Scholasticism treated reason as a threat to faith that needed to be suppressed.
questions.explanation: False. Anselm's own motto -- faith seeking understanding -- already states the opposite: reason works from within faith, deepening it, not undermining or replacing it. This is the same confidence in reason's compatibility with faith that later shapes Leo XIII's own commendation of Aquinas.
questions.hint: Recall Anselm's own motto from earlier in this level.

questions.prompt: What institution, described in the previous level, made large-scale scholastic debate and teaching like Aquinas's and Bonaventure's practically possible?
choices: The medieval university
The monastery alone, with no other institution involved
The royal court of the reigning king
The papal curia in Rome, acting alone
questions.explanation: Scholasticism did not happen in a vacuum -- it is, in a real sense, the intellectual product of the university system level 12 introduced, where mendicant friars like Aquinas and Bonaventure taught, debated, and wrote.
questions.hint: This is the same institution level 12 just described in detail.

questions.prompt: Even as Scholasticism was flourishing at the height of the medieval university system, what real institutional crisis was quietly building within the papacy itself?
choices: A series of pressures that would soon move the papacy to Avignon and later split it between rival claimants
No institutional tension of any kind existed within the papacy during this entire period
The papacy had already permanently relocated to Constantinople by this point
The office of the papacy itself had been formally abolished
questions.correctAnswer: A series of pressures that would soon move the papacy to Avignon and later split it between rival claimants
questions.explanation: Intellectual flourishing and institutional crisis run side by side in this period -- the next level turns from Scholasticism's confident synthesis to a genuinely painful chapter: the Avignon Papacy and the Western Schism.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: From 1309 to 1377, where did the papacy actually reside, rather than in Rome?
choices: Avignon, in France
Constantinople
Milan
Jerusalem
questions.explanation: For nearly seventy years, under heavy French political influence, a series of popes governed the Church from Avignon rather than Rome -- a real institutional crisis, not a minor administrative detail, and a stark contrast to the intellectual confidence of level 13's Scholasticism.
questions.hint: This is a city in southern France, not in Italy.

questions.prompt: St. Catherine of Siena, a laywoman with no formal theological education, is remembered for what documented action regarding the Avignon Papacy?
choices: Writing to and personally urging Pope Gregory XI to return the papacy to Rome
Founding the first Dominican convent in France
Serving as an official court theologian to the King of France
Translating the whole Bible into Italian
questions.correctAnswer: Writing to and personally urging Pope Gregory XI to return the papacy to Rome
questions.explanation: Catherine's letters and personal visits are historically documented and credited with helping persuade Gregory XI to end the Avignon Papacy and return to Rome in 1377 -- a specific, traceable action, not a vague reputation for wisdom.
questions.hint: Her persistent correspondence and personal visits are a real, documented factor in a pope's actual decision.

citations.quote: Mary is the perfect Orans (pray-er), a figure of the Church.

questions.prompt: Catherine of Siena's letters contributed to Pope Gregory XI's decision to return the papacy to ____ in 1377, ending the Avignon period.
questions.explanation: This is a rare case where a single laywoman's spiritual authority, exercised through nothing more than persistent letters and personal visits, had a concrete, traceable effect on the papacy's own institutional history.
questions.hint: The city the papacy had been absent from for nearly seventy years.

questions.prompt: True or False: The papacy's return to Rome in 1377 immediately and completely resolved the institutional crisis of this period, with no further complications.
questions.explanation: False. Within a year, disputed elections produced rival claimant popes -- the Western Schism -- meaning the return to Rome actually opened a new and even more confusing chapter rather than closing the crisis.
questions.hint: Consider what happened almost immediately after Gregory XI's return, in the very next papal election.

questions.prompt: At its worst point, how many men simultaneously claimed to be the true pope during the Western Schism?
choices: Three
One
Five
Two dozen
questions.explanation: By 1409, competing elections and failed attempts to resolve the dispute had produced three simultaneous claimants -- a scandal that made the question of legitimate authority urgently practical, not merely theoretical, for ordinary Christians trying to know which pope to obey.
questions.hint: Competing elections eventually produced more than two rival claimants.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or event of this level to what it involved.

pairs.right: The papacy residing in France, not Rome, for nearly seventy years
A laywoman whose letters helped bring the papacy back to Rome
Rival claimants simultaneously claiming to be the true pope
The council that finally resolved the schism and elected one pope

questions.explanation: This whole sequence -- exile, a laywoman's intervention, schism, and finally a council's resolution -- is one continuous institutional crisis, not four unrelated events, stretching across roughly a full century.
questions.hint: Follow the crisis in order: where the papacy went, who helped bring it back, what went wrong next, and how it was finally fixed.

questions.prompt: True or False: John Wycliffe's teachings, condemned at the Council of Constance, included a denial of transubstantiation.
questions.explanation: True. Wycliffe denied that the Eucharistic bread and wine truly become Christ's Body and Blood, and also attacked papal authority and Church-authorized interpretation of Scripture -- positions the Reformation would echo more than a century later.
questions.hint: This is the same Eucharistic doctrine Trent would later reaffirm, in a level still ahead.

questions.prompt: Jan Hus, influenced by Wycliffe's ideas, was summoned to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct. What actually happened to him there?
choices: He was condemned for heresy and burned at the stake in 1415
He was fully exonerated and reinstated to his teaching position
He successfully defended every one of his teachings before the council
He was quietly released and allowed to return home unharmed
questions.correctAnswer: He was condemned for heresy and burned at the stake in 1415
questions.explanation: Hus's execution, despite the promised safe conduct, left lasting bitterness in Bohemia and fed a Hussite movement that persisted for generations -- a foretaste of how explosively unresolved reform grievances could turn, a full century before Luther.
questions.hint: His fate at Constance, despite an official promise, left lasting bitterness in his homeland.

questions.prompt: The Council of ____ (1414-1418) finally resolved the Western Schism, deposing or accepting the resignation of the rival claimants and electing a single pope, Martin V.
questions.explanation: The same council that condemned Wycliffe and executed Hus also, in its central and most lasting achievement, finally ended decades of confusion over who the true pope actually was.
questions.hint: The German city this whole council, and its resolution of the schism, is named after.

questions.prompt: Having just resolved one severe institutional crisis at Constance, what does the Church face barely a century later, in the very next level of this topic?
choices: The Protestant Reformation, met with the Church's own response at the Council of Trent
A second, entirely identical Western Schism with new rival papal claimants
A complete and permanent dissolution of the papal office itself, once and for all
No further institutional or doctrinal challenges of any real kind whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: The Protestant Reformation, met with the Church's own response at the Council of Trent
questions.explanation: The unresolved grievances Hus's execution left simmering -- clerical corruption, unclear authority, popular anger -- did not simply disappear once Constance ended the schism; they resurface, on a much larger scale, when Luther posts his theses roughly a century later.
questions.hint: Consider what unresolved tensions from this level might still be simmering a century later.

citations.quote: [Each church shall] maintain, educate religiously, and train in ecclesiastical discipline a certain number of youths of their city and diocese.

questions.prompt: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) was convened by the Catholic Church primarily in response to what?
choices: The Protestant Reformation
The Great Schism of 1054
The Investiture Controversy
The Islamic conquest of Spain
questions.explanation: Trent clarified Catholic doctrine on Scripture, grace, and the sacraments against Reformation-era challenges, while also reforming clerical discipline and education -- the direct answer to the crisis level 14 left simmering.
questions.hint: This 16th-century movement, started by Luther, is what Trent was responding to.

citations.quote: [Each church shall] maintain, educate religiously, and train in ecclesiastical discipline a certain number of youths of their city and diocese.

questions.prompt: In 1517, what action did Martin Luther take that is traditionally remembered as sparking the Reformation?
choices: Posting Ninety-Five Theses criticizing the sale of indulgences to the door of Wittenberg's church
Personally assassinating a reigning pope in an act of open rebellion
Founding an entirely new university system across the German lands
Leading an organized armed uprising directly against the ruling Holy Roman Emperor himself
questions.correctAnswer: Posting Ninety-Five Theses criticizing the sale of indulgences to the door of Wittenberg's church
questions.explanation: Luther's theses, intended as an academic challenge to debate, spread rapidly thanks to the printing press and ignited a movement far larger than Luther himself initially intended -- the beginning of the crisis Trent will spend the rest of this level responding to.
questions.hint: This is a specific, documented act of academic protest, not a military one.

citations.quote: [Each church shall] maintain, educate religiously, and train in ecclesiastical discipline a certain number of youths of their city and diocese.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Council of Trent affirmed that both Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition hand on divine revelation.
questions.explanation: Against the Reformation principle of Scripture alone, Trent taught that revelation comes to the Church through both Scripture and Tradition together -- a direct doctrinal answer, not simply an administrative one, to the Reformation's core claim.
questions.hint: Trent rejected the Reformation idea that revelation flows through only one of these two sources.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament... as also the said traditions.

questions.prompt: Against the Reformation principle of 'sola fide' (faith alone), the Council of Trent taught that justification involves what?
choices: A real, interior transformation by grace, received through faith working together with love, not faith alone
Something earned entirely by good works alone, without any need for grace whatsoever
A change that happens automatically at birth for every single person without exception
A state that, once received, can never afterward be lost under any circumstance
questions.correctAnswer: A real, interior transformation by grace, received through faith working together with love, not faith alone
questions.explanation: Trent's Decree on Justification taught that grace truly renews and sanctifies the believer inwardly -- not merely God treating a sinner as righteous while nothing actually changes within.
questions.hint: Trent insisted something real actually changes inside the believer, not just a legal declaration.

citations.reference: Council of Trent (1545-1563), Decree on Justification
citations.quote: If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification... let him be anathema.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Council of Trent required the founding of seminaries to improve the education and discipline of parish priests.
questions.explanation: Trent's reforms directly addressed widespread clerical ignorance and laxity by mandating formal seminary training for future priests -- the exact institutional gap level 14's crisis had left exposed for generations.
questions.hint: Poorly trained clergy was a major problem Trent set out to fix through formal training.

citations.quote: [Each church shall] maintain, educate religiously, and train in ecclesiastical discipline a certain number of youths of their city and diocese.

questions.prompt: True or False: In 1566, Trent's Roman Catechism was published chiefly for parish priests, not for children meeting the faith for the first time.
questions.explanation: True. The Roman Catechism, or Catechism of the Council of Trent, was written as a resource for pastors preaching and instructing others -- its tone assumes a reader who must explain the faith to others, not one meeting it for the first time.
questions.hint: Consider who most needed a reliable, standardized reference in a period of contested preaching.

questions.prompt: Trent-era Rome also maintained an ____ of Forbidden Books, listing works Catholics were instructed not to read without special permission.
questions.explanation: The Index, formally established in this same era and maintained for centuries afterward, reflects the period's real anxiety about controlling access to Reformation-era writings -- a disciplinary tool distinct from Trent's positive doctrinal and formational work covered elsewhere in this level.
questions.hint: The word for an official list -- in this case, of books Catholics were instructed to avoid.

questions.prompt: The Council of Trent's decree establishing seminaries addressed what practical problem in the pre-Reformation Church?
choices: Many parish priests were poorly educated and inconsistently formed, since there was no standard system for training clergy
There were, at the time, simply too many ordained priests relative to the total lay population
Priests of this period were formally and entirely forbidden from receiving any theological education
Seminaries of this kind already existed everywhere and Trent's decree only renamed them
questions.correctAnswer: Many parish priests were poorly educated and inconsistently formed, since there was no standard system for training clergy
questions.explanation: Poor clerical formation was a real and serious contributor to the crisis the Reformation exposed. Trent's seminary decree was not a side note to its doctrinal work -- it was a direct structural response to a genuine failure, and dioceses still operate seminaries built on this decree today.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of training existed for parish priests before this decree.

questions.prompt: Even as Trent was reforming the Church at home, what was happening at the same time on a much wider, global scale?
choices: Catholic missionaries were carrying the faith to newly reached lands in Asia and the Americas
The Church was deliberately withdrawing entirely from any activity outside of Europe
All missionary activity had permanently and completely ceased since the apostolic era
Europe had lost essentially all contact with the wider world during this whole period
questions.correctAnswer: Catholic missionaries were carrying the faith to newly reached lands in Asia and the Americas
questions.explanation: Trent's internal renewal and a real global missionary expansion happen side by side in this same century -- the next level turns to that missionary story directly, including the real cultural questions it raised.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic turns to.

questions.prompt: St. Francis Xavier, one of the original companions of St. Ignatius of Loyola, is remembered chiefly for what missionary work in the 16th century?
choices: Carrying the Gospel to India and Japan, opening a new era of missionary expansion into Asia
Leading the Council of Trent's own detailed doctrinal deliberations in person, on site
Founding the very first medieval university anywhere in the whole of Europe itself
Personally translating the entire Christian Bible directly into the Mandarin Chinese language
questions.correctAnswer: Carrying the Gospel to India and Japan, opening a new era of missionary expansion into Asia
questions.explanation: Xavier's mission opened the era this level covers -- Jesuit missionaries carrying the faith across Asia, raising real, difficult questions about how far local custom could be adapted without compromising the faith itself.
questions.hint: This missionary's own feast day, December 3, honors work done specifically in Asia.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: Matteo Ricci's missionary method in China -- permitting converts to retain certain ancestral and civil ceremonies as culturally rather than religiously binding -- became known to history as the policy of ____.
questions.explanation: Ricci's method tried to distinguish civil and ancestral customs from strictly religious worship, arguing the former could remain compatible with Catholic faith -- a policy this same level shows was eventually reversed by Rome.
questions.hint: The same word describes adapting an approach to fit a new situation.

questions.prompt: True or False: In Ex Illa Die (1715), Pope Clement XI approved the Jesuit practice of allowing Chinese Catholics to continue traditional rites honoring Confucius and their ancestors, judging them compatible with the Catholic faith.
questions.explanation: Ex Illa Die did the opposite: it upheld the earlier condemnation of the Chinese Rites, ruling that the ancestral and Confucian ceremonies could not be permitted for Catholics -- a decision that effectively ended the accommodation method Ricci had begun.
questions.hint: The pope's ruling ended, rather than approved, this contested missionary practice.

questions.prompt: What was the core question at issue in the Chinese Rites controversy?
choices: Whether Chinese Catholic converts could continue certain ancestral honoring and Confucian civic rites alongside their new faith
Whether Chinese converts needed to formally learn to read and write Latin before receiving baptism
Whether Catholic missionaries should be permitted to enter the country of China at all, under any circumstance
Whether the reigning Chinese Emperor himself could personally be baptized into the Catholic faith
questions.correctAnswer: Whether Chinese Catholic converts could continue certain ancestral honoring and Confucian civic rites alongside their new faith
questions.explanation: Jesuit missionaries argued these rites were civic and familial customs rather than religious worship of false gods, and so compatible with the faith; other missionary orders disagreed sharply. Rome eventually sided against the accommodation, with lasting consequences for the mission's reception in China.
questions.hint: The dispute concerns which practices count as religious worship versus civic custom.

questions.prompt: True or False: A closely parallel accommodation controversy over the 'Malabar Rites' arose in India around the missionary Roberto de Nobili, echoing the Chinese Rites dispute.
questions.explanation: True. De Nobili, another Jesuit, adopted local customs and dress to reach India's higher castes, raising the same core question this level has already explored in China: where is the line between adaptable custom and compromised faith? Rome eventually restricted this practice too, on similar grounds.
questions.hint: This controversy involves the same missionary order, applying a similar strategy in a different country.

questions.explanation: A single real question -- how far can the Gospel adapt to local custom without compromising itself -- runs through every figure and document in this level, on two different continents.
questions.hint: Three are missionaries or their methods; one is Rome's eventual ruling on the question.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Jesuit reducciones in Paraguay were mission settlements that gave the indigenous Guaraní a significant degree of self-governance, relatively protected from colonial exploitation.
questions.explanation: True. The reducciones organized community life, agriculture, and defense with real Guaraní participation, and were frequently in tension with colonial slavers and settlers who wanted access to that labor and land -- proof that missionary work in this period was not simply an extension of colonial power.
questions.hint: Ask who benefited from these settlements existing, and who wanted them gone.

questions.prompt: What does the pattern across this whole level -- India and Japan, China, and Paraguay -- suggest about Catholic missionary work in this period?
choices: It was a genuine, wide-ranging global expansion, raising real and difficult questions about adapting the faith to radically different cultures
It was strictly limited to a single country alone, with no wider geographic reach of any kind whatsoever
It always simply imposed European customs wholesale on converts, with no genuine attempt at real cultural adaptation
It had no real relationship whatsoever to the wider political and colonial context of its own historical era
questions.correctAnswer: It was a genuine, wide-ranging global expansion, raising real and difficult questions about adapting the faith to radically different cultures
questions.explanation: Three continents, one recurring question: how much can and should the Gospel adapt to a genuinely different culture? This level does not pretend Rome's answers were simple or uncontested -- the Chinese and Malabar Rites controversies show real, sustained internal disagreement.
questions.hint: Consider what India, Japan, China, and Paraguay all have in common as settings for this same level.

questions.prompt: Rome's rulings on the Chinese and Malabar Rites controversies show the Church exercising real, ongoing ____ over how far missionary adaptation could go, not leaving the question purely to individual missionaries.
questions.explanation: Even genuinely well-intentioned missionary strategy, developed on the ground by dedicated men, remained subject to the wider Church's own discernment and final judgment -- a real check this level shows was actually exercised, not merely claimed.
questions.hint: What the wider Church exercised over missionary strategy that individual missionaries could not simply decide on their own.

questions.prompt: While these missionary questions were unfolding abroad, what kind of disputes were unfolding within Europe itself during roughly this same period?
choices: Serious internal disputes over grace and free will, and growing political pressure against the Jesuit order itself
No internal disputes of any real or serious kind existed anywhere within Europe during this whole period
A complete and total absence of theological disagreement across the entire Church at this time
Disputes that concerned exclusively foreign missionary policy abroad and nothing whatsoever besides that
questions.correctAnswer: Serious internal disputes over grace and free will, and growing political pressure against the Jesuit order itself
questions.explanation: The next level turns from the missionary frontier back to Europe's own internal life -- Jansenism's rigorist theology of grace, and the mounting political pressure that would culminate in the Jesuits' 1773 suppression, the same order whose missionaries this level has just followed across three continents.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: Pope Clement XI's 1713 bull Unigenitus condemned 101 propositions drawn from the writings of Pasquier Quesnel. Which movement's rigorist teaching on grace and free will did these propositions represent?
choices: Jansenism
Pelagianism
Quietism
Modernism
questions.explanation: Jansenism held that grace acts on the will in a way that leaves no real freedom to resist it, effectively denying that a person can freely cooperate with or reject grace. Unigenitus condemned this rigorist account as incompatible with the Church's teaching on grace and human freedom.
questions.hint: This movement takes its name from a 17th-century Flemish bishop who wrote a massive treatise on St. Augustine.

questions.prompt: What did the Gallican Articles of 1682, adopted by the French clergy under royal pressure, assert about the relationship between councils and the Pope?
choices: That a general council's authority could, in certain respects, stand above the Pope's own
That the reigning Pope's own authority was entirely unlimited in every single respect
That France itself should formally and permanently separate from the Catholic Church
That bishops held no real authority independent of Rome's own authority at all
questions.correctAnswer: That a general council's authority could, in certain respects, stand above the Pope's own
questions.explanation: Gallicanism echoes the conciliarist theory level 14 already introduced during the Western Schism -- a real, recurring tension over where final authority rests, here driven as much by French royal politics as by theology.
questions.hint: This is the same underlying theory level 14 already introduced, applied again here under different political pressure.

questions.prompt: True or False: Jansenism's rigorist theology of grace had no real practical effect on ordinary Catholic devotional life, remaining a purely academic theological dispute.
questions.explanation: False. Jansenist rigorism shaped real pastoral practice for generations -- discouraging frequent Communion and confession out of a severe view of human unworthiness -- effects still being undone well into the 19th and 20th centuries by popes encouraging more frequent reception of the sacraments.
questions.hint: Consider what this movement's severe view of grace and human worthiness would do to how often ordinary Catholics felt able to receive the sacraments.

questions.prompt: What ultimately led to Pope Clement XIV's 1773 suppression of the Society of Jesus?
choices: Sustained political pressure from several European monarchies who saw the Jesuits as a threat to royal authority and colonial economic interests
A formal doctrinal condemnation of Jesuit theology, issued directly and explicitly by a sitting ecumenical council of bishops
The Society of Jesus's own entirely voluntary, freely and formally made request that it be dissolved outright
An official Vatican finding that the Society had fully abandoned its own vow of obedience to the reigning Pope
questions.correctAnswer: Sustained political pressure from several European monarchies who saw the Jesuits as a threat to royal authority and colonial economic interests
questions.explanation: This was fundamentally a political suppression rather than a doctrinal condemnation -- Bourbon monarchs in France, Spain, and Portugal pressed for it over years, and Clement XIV yielded to preserve peace with those courts. The reducciones and missions this topic's previous level described were part of what made the Jesuits politically vulnerable.
questions.hint: Ask whether this was a doctrinal finding, or a matter of political pressure from outside the Church.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Society of Jesus survived in one country despite the 1773 suppression, because its ruler declined to publish Clement XIV's brief there.
questions.explanation: True. Catherine the Great of Russia declined to publish Dominus ac Redemptor within her territory, allowing a remnant of the Jesuit order to survive there continuously until the order's full, worldwide restoration in 1814.
questions.hint: This survival happened in a country outside Catholic Europe's usual political sphere.

questions.prompt: The Society of Jesus, suppressed in 1773, was fully and formally restored worldwide in the year ____, once the political pressure that caused its suppression had passed.
questions.explanation: The restoration confirms what this level has already suggested: the suppression was a political concession, not a lasting doctrinal judgment against the order or its mission work.
questions.hint: This restoration happens after the Napoleonic Wars, in the early 19th century.

questions.prompt: Weighing Jansenism, Gallicanism, and the Jesuit suppression together, what pattern does this level reveal about the 17th and 18th centuries?
choices: Sustained internal theological rigorism and growing state pressure both tested Rome's authority from different directions at once
The Church faced no internal or external challenges of any kind during this whole period
Every dispute in this period was purely a matter of state politics with no theological content whatsoever
Every dispute in this period was purely theological with no political dimension whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: Sustained internal theological rigorism and growing state pressure both tested Rome's authority from different directions at once
questions.explanation: Jansenism was a theological rigorism Rome had to condemn from within; Gallicanism and the Jesuit suppression were driven heavily by outside state pressure. Distinguishing the two kinds of challenge matters for judging how much of this history is properly doctrinal.
questions.hint: Ask which of these three came primarily from theology, and which came primarily from royal courts.

questions.prompt: Match each 18th-century episode to what it actually concerned.

Yielding to sustained pressure from European monarchies

questions.explanation: Two of these are the Church teaching from within; two are the Church responding to, and eventually outlasting, external political pressure -- a distinction worth carrying forward into the revolutionary upheaval the next level covers.
questions.hint: Two of these four are theological corrections; two are political events with a later reversal.

questions.prompt: The kind of state pressure that forced the Jesuits' suppression in 1773 was about to intensify dramatically. What major political upheaval does the next level turn to?
choices: The French Revolution and its direct, often violent assault on the Church in France
A complete and total end to any tension between Church and state anywhere in Europe
The permanent restoration of the Papal States to their largest historical extent
A second Council of Trent convened to address the same 16th-century controversies again
questions.correctAnswer: The French Revolution and its direct, often violent assault on the Church in France
questions.explanation: The Bourbon monarchies that pressured Clement XIV against the Jesuits would themselves soon face a revolution that turned violently against the Church itself -- the next level's central subject, and a far more severe test of the same underlying question: who holds legitimate authority, and on what basis.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the very monarchies that pressured the Jesuits' suppression, within a generation.

questions.prompt: The French Revolution's 1790 Civil Constitution of the Clergy attempted what, which most French bishops and priests ultimately refused to accept?
choices: Placing the French Church under state control, with bishops and priests elected by civil authorities rather than confirmed by Rome
Simply granting the French Church a somewhat greater degree of financial independence from the reigning state
Formally and fully restoring all Church property that had been seized by the crown in earlier centuries
Reuniting the entire French Church with the Church of England under one single unified structure
questions.correctAnswer: Placing the French Church under state control, with bishops and priests elected by civil authorities rather than confirmed by Rome
questions.explanation: The Civil Constitution demanded clergy swear an oath to this new state-controlled structure; most refused, splitting French clergy into 'juring' and 'non-juring' priests and setting the Revolution directly against a Church it saw as a rival source of authority.
questions.hint: Ask who this document put in charge of appointing bishops and priests -- Rome, or the revolutionary state.

questions.prompt: True or False: During the Revolution's most radical phase, the Reign of Terror, thousands of priests and religious were imprisoned, exiled, or executed for refusing the new state-controlled Church structure.
questions.explanation: True. Refusal to take the state's oath was treated as counter-revolutionary, and non-juring clergy faced imprisonment, exile, or execution -- a real, documented persecution, not a minor administrative dispute.
questions.hint: Consider what happened to clergy who refused the oath this level's first question described.

questions.prompt: In 1794, sixteen Discalced Carmelite nuns of Compiègne were guillotined for refusing to abandon their religious vows, going to their deaths singing the ____ -- a hymn of praise to God.
questions.explanation: Their calm witness -- singing rather than pleading -- became one of the most vivid remembered images of this whole period's persecution, later inspiring the opera Dialogues of the Carmelites.
questions.hint: A traditional Marian hymn, sung by these nuns even as they faced execution.

citations.quote: Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death.

questions.prompt: In 1801, Napoleon Bonaparte negotiated a Concordat with the papacy that did what?
choices: Formally reconciled the French state and the Catholic Church, restoring public Catholic worship in France after a decade of persecution
Permanently and completely abolished the Catholic Church throughout the whole of the French nation
Permanently and completely abolished the practice of the Catholic Church throughout the whole of the French nation entirely
United the entire French Church with the German-speaking Church under a single presiding bishop
questions.correctAnswer: Formally reconciled the French state and the Catholic Church, restoring public Catholic worship in France after a decade of persecution
questions.explanation: Napoleon, seeking stability rather than religious conviction, negotiated a formal reconciliation that ended the worst of the Revolution's anti-Church persecution -- though he also retained significant state control over Church appointments, keeping real tension alive underneath the formal peace.
questions.hint: This agreement ends open persecution, though it does not remove every tension between Paris and Rome.

questions.prompt: True or False: Napoleon's 1801 Concordat, though it ended open persecution, still gave the French state real ongoing influence over the Church's affairs.
questions.explanation: True. Napoleon retained the right to nominate bishops for papal confirmation and kept clergy on the state payroll -- a real, ongoing state entanglement, not a full and clean return to the Church's pre-Revolutionary independence.
questions.hint: Consider whether Napoleon fully gave up state control over Church appointments, or only partially.

questions.prompt: True or False: After Napoleon's fall, the Congress of Vienna (1815) restored much of Europe's older political order, including the Papal States' territory in Italy.
questions.explanation: True. The Vienna settlement rolled back many of the Revolution's and Napoleon's changes, restoring the Papal States and much of the old European order -- though the ideas the Revolution had unleashed, nationalism and liberalism among them, did not simply disappear with a treaty.
questions.hint: This settlement comes after Napoleon's final defeat, and deliberately looks backward toward the pre-Revolutionary order.

questions.prompt: Did the political restoration after 1815 fully resolve the tensions the Revolution had exposed between the Church and the modern liberal state?
choices: No -- restoring old borders did not undo the new liberal and nationalist ideas the Revolution had spread, which kept challenging the Church's position for decades afterward
Yes -- the 1815 restoration completely and permanently ended any and all tension between the Church and liberal or nationalist movements everywhere
Yes, but only because liberalism and nationalism as movements had already fully disappeared on their own by 1815
No -- but only because the Congress of Vienna actually abolished the Papal States outright rather than restoring them
questions.correctAnswer: No -- restoring old borders did not undo the new liberal and nationalist ideas the Revolution had spread, which kept challenging the Church's position for decades afterward
questions.explanation: A map can be redrawn faster than ideas can be unlearned -- the liberal and nationalist movements the Revolution helped unleash kept pressing against the Church's traditional position throughout the 19th century, which is exactly where the next level picks up.
questions.hint: Distinguish what a treaty can restore (borders, thrones) from what it cannot simply undo (ideas already spread).

questions.prompt: The Revolution's central claim -- that legitimate authority flows upward from the people's own will rather than downward from God -- placed it in direct tension with the Church's own teaching on the true source of all legitimate ____.
questions.explanation: This is the deepest question underneath every event in this level: where does legitimate authority actually come from? The Revolution answered one way; the Church, across the disputes this whole topic has already traced -- from Peter's own authority in level 1 to Gallicanism in level 17 -- has consistently answered another.
questions.hint: The thing the Revolution claimed came from the people, which the Church teaches ultimately comes from God.

A complete and final resolution of every single Church-state tension, reached immediately and permanently after 1815
A simple return to exactly the same disputes already fully covered back in level 8's account of Nicaea
An entirely unrelated subject bearing no real connection at all to this level's central question

questions.prompt: According to Pastor Aeternus (1870), which of the following is NOT one of the conditions required for a papal teaching to count as an infallible ex cathedra act?
choices: That it be issued after consultation with an ecumenical council currently in session
That the Pope speak in his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians
That he define a doctrine concerning faith or morals
That he intend the definition to be held by the whole Church
questions.correctAnswer: That it be issued after consultation with an ecumenical council currently in session
questions.explanation: Pastor Aeternus defines the conditions for an ex cathedra act: the Pope speaking in his supreme office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, by his supreme apostolic authority, defining a doctrine of faith or morals, intending it be held by the whole Church. No council needs to be in session -- his authority to do this is independent of conciliar consultation, exactly what Vatican I was defining against Gallican claims.
questions.hint: This is the same kind of conciliar dependency Gallicanism wanted and Vatican I rejected.

questions.prompt: True or False: Blessed Pope Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors (1864) listing the proposition that the Pope should 'reconcile himself to progress, liberalism, and modern civilization' among the condemned errors means the document is properly read as an outright condemnation of democratic government as such.
questions.explanation: The Syllabus does list that proposition (no. 80) -- but read in its actual context, its target was the ideological claim that the Church must subordinate her teaching to whatever 'modern civilization' currently holds, not democratic government or civil liberty as such. Later magisterial teaching, especially from Leo XIII onward, engaged constructively with modern political forms while keeping this same caution against doctrinal subordination.
questions.hint: The Syllabus targets a philosophical claim about the Church's independence, not a specific form of government.

questions.prompt: True or False: When the Kingdom of Italy annexed Rome in 1870, ending the Papal States, Pope Pius IX voluntarily transferred temporal governance to the new Italian government in exchange for guaranteed religious liberty.
questions.explanation: Pius IX transferred nothing voluntarily -- Italian troops took Rome by force in September 1870, and the Pope refused to recognize the seizure, considering himself a 'prisoner in the Vatican.' The dispute, called the Roman Question, was not resolved until the Lateran Treaty of 1929 established Vatican City as a sovereign state.

questions.prompt: Why did Pope Pius IX refuse to leave the Vatican after Rome was annexed by the Kingdom of Italy in 1870?
choices: He considered himself effectively a prisoner protesting the seizure of the Papal States, a status maintained by his successors until the 1929 Lateran Treaty
He was placed under a formal, legally imposed house arrest ordered directly and explicitly by the new Italian civil authorities
He had personally and publicly taken a private, binding vow never again to leave the grounds of the Vatican itself
Travel outside the city of Rome had been made explicitly and permanently forbidden to him under Italian civil law
questions.correctAnswer: He considered himself effectively a prisoner protesting the seizure of the Papal States, a status maintained by his successors until the 1929 Lateran Treaty
questions.explanation: This was a self-imposed protest, the 'prisoner of the Vatican' stance, not a legal detention — and it lasted nearly sixty years across four pontificates until Mussolini's government and the Holy See settled the Roman Question with the Lateran Treaty in 1929.
questions.hint: Ask whether this was imposed from outside, or a stance the popes themselves chose to maintain.
